Biological function is best understood etiologically because functions are normative: a trait can perform its function well or badly, and it can have a function even when it fails to perform it. Selected-effect accounts explain this by identifying a trait’s function with the effect for which earlier instances of that trait were selected. The function of the heart is to pump blood because ancestral hearts contributed to survival and reproduction by pumping blood, and that effect explains why hearts of that kind were preserved and reproduced in the lineage. This makes sense of malfunction. A diseased heart that fails to pump blood properly still has pumping blood as its function, because its function is fixed by the selection history of hearts, not by its present causal powers. By contrast, a purely dispositional analysis identifies function with what a trait is disposed to do, or with what it in fact does under certain conditions. Such an account cannot adequately distinguish functioning from malfunctioning. If a heart is disposed only to fibrillate, or if an eye is incapable of seeing, a purely dispositional account has difficulty explaining why these are defective instances rather than traits with different functions. Etiology supplies the missing standard: the trait is evaluated against the effect that explains its historical retention.

Causal-role accounts in the tradition of Cummins analyze function in terms of the contribution a component makes to the capacities of a containing system. On this view, the function of a trait is whatever causal role it plays in some larger explanatory analysis. But biological traits have many causal effects, and not all of them are functions. The heart pumps blood, makes sounds, adds weight to the body, consumes energy, and can obstruct a surgeon’s access to other organs. A causal-role analysis can call any of these a function if the chosen explanatory project makes that effect relevant. This means that the line between a function and an accidental effect depends on the investigator’s explanatory interests. If one is explaining circulation, pumping blood is selected; if one is explaining diagnostic auscultation, producing sounds is selected; if one is explaining body mass, contributing weight is selected. The attribution becomes relative to a chosen analysis rather than fixed by the biological history of the trait. Etiological accounts preserve objectivity by distinguishing the effect that explains the trait’s existence from the many effects the trait happens to have. The function is not whatever an investigator finds useful to cite, but the effect for which the trait was selected.

Etiological accounts also best explain why functional claims have distinctive explanatory force. To say that the function of the heart is to pump blood is not merely to describe a current activity of the heart. It is to answer why organisms have hearts of that type at all. The selected effect explains the presence and persistence of the trait in the lineage: hearts are there because ancestral hearts pumped blood in ways that contributed to reproductive success. This historical explanation is what gives functional language its biological depth. A purely causal-role statement says what a trait does within a system now; it locates the trait in an organized causal economy. But it does not by itself explain why that trait exists rather than not, or why organisms came to possess it. Etiological function does. It connects current organization to evolutionary history, showing how a trait’s present role is grounded in past selection. For that reason, functional claims in biology are most fully explanatory when they are etiological: they identify not merely an effect of the trait, but the effect that accounts for the trait’s being there.
